title: jay rayner responsibility restaurant criticism 2026 09 12
text:
Jay Rayner, by his own admission, doesn’t get invited to too many dinner parties.
The veteran British restaurant critic — whose more than a quarter-century of reviews for The Observer and, more recently, the Financial Times newspaper has earned him the nickname “Acid Rayner” — is known for his searing assessments of restaurants across the U.K. Among his most excoriating assessments was that he couldn’t describe one place as serving “the worst cooking in Britain,” if only because he hadn’t eaten in every restaurant in the land.
But Rayner’s day job doesn’t mean he’ll turn his nose up atgood old-fashioned home cooking, which he pays homage to in his latest book “Nights Out in the Kitchen,” a part-cookbook, part-memoir featuring recipes for some of the best dishes from across his career, plus some original dishes.
Speaking with Reuters from his home in South London ahead of his book tour, Rayner discusses the art of the review in the social media age, his philosophy for negative critiques, and the restaurants he won’t go near.
This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.
You’ve been a restaurant critic for more than a quarter century. How’d you get your start?
I’m a print journalist. That is the thing I've always been. I chose my university because it had the biggest student newspaper, got elected editor, and I was then a general writer and reporter, advancing from very soft features into harder and harder news and long form and foreign reporting. I did it all apart from sport — and even then, I like to point out that I once did the all-amateur natural bodybuilding championship in Leeds.
And then, (in 1999), I was taken out for lunch by the then editor of The Observer magazine, for whom I deputized on every column, and she said, "Our restaurant critic is moving on. Who should I get to do the job?" It was not my intention to put my hand up. But the moment she said that, I went, "Well, how about me?"
What I discovered in food was that it covers everything: politics, economics, history, trade routes. When people look at the Arab Spring, they see it as a spontaneous uprising in response to a sudden desire for democracy. But if you drill down on it, it's actually about food price rises and the inability of authoritarian governments to keep their population in line when they could no longer give them bread at a reasonable price. And when you start to understand that, you think, this is a really interesting subject. And so it has continually become a part of my working life.
Over 25 years, what's changed about what makes a good review? And what has stayed the same?
Has anything changed about what makes a good review? I don't think it has, actually. I think the eternal verities (remain true), which is that you have to speak to the reader as though they're the only person reading, that you are telling them how much pleasure their money will give them. You're not writing for the tiny number of well-informed gastronomes — the "napkin sniffers," as I call them — but for the general reader and you need to understand it as a conversation with those readers.
That said, a lot has changed about the way restaurants are covered, how much other coverage there is.
Social media has played a big part in that. With the rise of content creation, these days most anyone can be a critic. Do you see that as a challenge?
It is only a challenge if it's better than me. I cannot just claim, "Look, I'm the guy from the big newspaper and therefore I have a right to be read." Every writer has to make an argument for their writing to be read every single time they write. Nobody has to read a single thing you write — not even your mother.
There's a lot of stuff out there, and some of it's good and some of it's bad. Generally, I like to think that the audience will spot the rubbish. There are certain influencer review sites where I think, "Oh God, this is awful,” but it's got 2.5 million followers, so they must like something about it.
Your new book reads as part-cookbook, part memoir. What are you hoping readers take from it, apart from some delicious home cooking recipes?
This is the sequel to "Nights Out at Home," which happened because I was heading towards 25 years (as a restaurant critic), and what I realized was I genuinely have this habit of, if I come across a good idea in a restaurant, I'll take it home and reverse engineer that idea. I thought, actually, that's a brilliant way (of) telling the stories of these restaurants you love. It's a very broad selection of dishes, plus, with this one, 20 of the (recipes) are officially mine. They're things that I cook or have always cooked.
In one chapter, you reflect on some of the more brutal reviews you’ve given.
You mean the chapter headed, "Am I a total bastard?"
That's the one. It got me wondering: How do you approach writing a negative review? Have you ever returned to a restaurant that received one to see if it improved?
I've done it only once. It was a place where they’d advertised themselves as being a great Italian new wave restaurant. I went there and concluded it was just a bar, and they weren't really interested in the food. That was the review. The owner wrote to me and said, "You're absolutely right, but we are now," and I went back and it was.
The interesting thing, at least to me, is I wouldn't have bothered with that first review now. If I'd gone there and had that experience, I would have paid the bill and never written about it. So the major difference now, and I think it's a lot to do with COVID and coming out of (the pandemic), is if you're going to write a negative review, you better have a bloody good reason for it. And the motto is: punch up, not down.
The small mom-and-pop place that's not doing very well or isn't making it, let them fail by themselves. But if you come across somewhere like (the high-end London restaurant) Jul's — this mad, insane place apparently born out of some landmark restaurant in Ibiza where they were doing terrible things to the food at excruciating prices, I didn't have any concerns about writing what I felt. And the point I said in the review was: money might end up being spent here that should be spent elsewhere. Now that's a bit brutal, but it's true.
You write about the #MeToo reckoning in kitchens. Has that changed how you review a restaurant — what you're looking for, what you're weighing?
It is complicated because, generally, you do not know what's going on in a restaurant. It's like a family: You can't necessarily tell it's dysfunctional if you just go over for tea. Maybe you can sense it.
There are certain chefs I will not review because I think they're monstrous individuals. If you are a nightmarish figure, I'm not going near you. That all sounds very grand and moral. The problem is you can't always tell.
What kinds of cuisines do you think are still unrepresented or underrepresented in the places you review?
The entirety of Africa. We obviously have very developed African communities in the U.K., but the restaurants representing the food of Africa tend to be mediated in some way. Sichuan food (in London) will bear similarities to what you find in Chengdu, whereas a Nigerian restaurant that ends up in Soho is unlikely to be what you'll find in the back streets of Lagos. I'm not sure why that is.
Now for some rapid-fire questions. What’s your death-row meal?
You can find it in my book, "My Last Supper: One Meal, a Lifetime in the Making." It would involve garlicky snails, a bacon sandwich properly made on white bread, and a Mont Blanc to finish.
Who would you invite to your dream dinner party?
Dorothy Parker, but only until the end of the starters, because after that she'll be drunk and just a bit annoying. Peter Ustinov, who was a great British actor, wit, and raconteur. Ella Fitzgerald, because I have a sideline as a jazz pianist and I'd love to play alongside her. Gene Harris, who is a fantastic, bluesy jazz pianist. And if I'm allowed fictional, Baloo the Bear from "The Jungle Book."
Another is Dita Von Teese. After Dorothy Parker has had to retire, Dita can take over.
What’s your favorite restaurant of late?
My most recent top experience is a place called IGNI. It is a live-fire tasting menu restaurant (in London) by a chef called Theo Clench. I normally have no time or patience for the whole tasting menu thing — I find it tiresome and performative, and all the performance doesn't match up to the joy of the food. But this one really, really did.
